subject: Architecture
title: Korean Palace Architecture: Harmony with Nature
description: A micro-lesson that makes Korean Palace Architecture: Harmony with Nature usable.

hook.text: Korean palaces weren't built to dominate nature. They were designed to blend into it.

buildup.text: Gyeongbokgung Palace was aligned with mountains behind and water in front, following feng shui.

discovery.text: Ondol, Korea's underfloor heating, piped hot air beneath stone floors — invented 2,500 years ago.

twist.text: Japan destroyed the palace in 1592. Korea rebuilt it. Japan demolished it again in 1910. Korea rebuilt again.

climax.text: Today's restoration used original tools and methods, rejecting modern shortcuts entirely.

punchline.text: Burned twice. Rebuilt twice. A palace that refuses to disappear.

quiz.question: What is ondol in Korean architecture?
options: A curved roof style inspired by dragon scales
An underfloor heating system using hot air
A decorative gate marking the palace entrance

details.summary: Korean palace architecture, exemplified by Seoul's Gyeongbokgung, was designed to harmonize with surrounding mountains and water according to pungsu (Korean geomancy) principles.
details.whyItMatters: Korean palatial design shows that monumental architecture doesn't require dominating nature. The integration of buildings with topography demonstrates an alternative to Western traditions of imposing geometric order on landscapes.
takeaways: Gyeongbokgung Palace follows pungsu geomantic principles
Buildings align with mountains and water features naturally
Architecture integrates with landscape rather than dominating it

faq.question: What is pungsu and how does it affect architecture?
faq.answer: Pungsu (wind and water) is Korean geomancy, similar to Chinese feng shui. It determines optimal building placement based on mountain orientation, water flow, and energy patterns. Gyeongbokgung faces south with mountains behind and water before it, following ideal pungsu principles.

faq.question: How does Korean palace design differ from Chinese?
faq.answer: While influenced by Chinese architecture, Korean palaces use less rigid symmetry, integrate more closely with natural topography, and employ gentler roof curves. The relationship between buildings and their natural setting is given more emphasis than in the strictly axial Chinese model.
